passages.text: A student investigated whether covering soil with mulch helps it hold water. She filled four identical trays with the same soil, covered three of them with different materials, left one uncovered, watered all four equally, and measured the soil's moisture five days later. She concluded that the benefit of mulch depends greatly on the material used, noting that ______

table.title: Soil moisture after five days

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the tray covered with straw held about twice as much moisture as the uncovered tray.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the tray covered with gravel held only slightly more moisture than the uncovered tray, while the tray covered with straw held about twice as much.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the trays covered with straw and with wood chips both held more moisture than the uncovered tray.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the uncovered tray held less moisture than any of the covered trays.

content.explanation: The conclusion is that the benefit depends on the material, so the evidence must contrast materials with very different effects. Gravel raised moisture only from 12% to 13%, while straw raised it to 24%, about twice the uncovered tray. Choice B shows that contrast.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is accurate but describes only one material, so it shows mulch can help, not that the benefit depends on the material.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is accurate but shows two materials that both helped a lot, which doesn't show a large difference between materials.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is accurate but supports only the general claim that covering soil helps.

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central Market station averaged 410 riders per weekday, the most of any station.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Riverside station averaged 340 riders per weekend day, compared with 150 riders per weekday.

choices.label: C
choices.text: University station averaged 380 riders per weekday but only 120 riders per weekend day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hilltop station had the fewest riders of the four stations on both weekdays and weekends.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it is about Hilltop and doesn't show Riverside being busier on weekends.

passages.text: Historian Grace Whitlock studies how work changed in Alder County during the twentieth century. As farming employed a smaller and smaller share of the county's workers, other kinds of jobs grew. Whitlock argues that between 1900 and 1960, the decline in farm jobs was offset mainly by growth in service jobs, not manufacturing jobs.

table.title: Share of jobs in Alder County by sector (%)

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Whitlock's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From 1900 to 1930, manufacturing's share of jobs grew by 12 percentage points, while the share of service jobs grew by only 6 points.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In 1930, the shares of jobs in manufacturing and in services were nearly equal, at 33% each.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Agriculture's share of jobs was smaller in each year shown than in the previous year shown.

choices.label: D
choices.text: From 1900 to 1960, agriculture's share of jobs fell by 40 percentage points, while the share of service jobs rose by 26 points and manufacturing's share rose by 14 points.

content.explanation: Whitlock's argument covers 1900 to 1960 and says service jobs, more than manufacturing jobs, replaced farm jobs. Over that whole period, agriculture fell from 52% to 12% (40 points), services rose from 27% to 53% (26 points), and manufacturing rose from 21% to 35% (14 points). Services gained nearly twice as much as manufacturing, so choice D supports the argument.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it covers only 1900 to 1930, when manufacturing grew faster than services. It points away from Whitlock's argument.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it describes a single year and shows no change over time.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it shows only that farm jobs declined, not which kind of job grew more to replace them.

passages.text: In 2018, a drained wetland was restored by blocking the ditches that had carried its water away. Volunteer surveyor Dana Whitfield compared bird counts from before and after the restoration. She concluded that the restoration has favored some species while others have fared worse since then: ______

table.title: Bird counts at a restored wetland

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: great egret counts more than doubled, from 48 to 112, while red-winged blackbird counts fell by half, from 520 to 260.

choices.label: B
choices.text: great egret and wood duck counts both roughly doubled between 2015 and 2024.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the mallard count fell slightly, from 310 in 2015 to 295 in 2024.

choices.label: D
choices.text: red-winged blackbirds were the most numerous of the four species in 2015.

content.explanation: Whitfield's conclusion has two parts: some species did better and others did worse. Choice A shows both: great egrets went from 48 to 112 (more than double), while red-winged blackbirds dropped from 520 to 260 (half). The other choices show only one side or neither.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it shows only species that increased, not any that fared worse.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it shows only one species that declined slightly, not any species that was favored.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it describes only the 2015 count and shows no change at all.

passages.text: Sociologist Ana Petrovic surveyed commuters in one city about how they would most like to get to work. She reports that a preference for cycling was far more common among younger respondents than older ones. But she cautions that this does not make cycling the younger group's top choice: ______

table.title: Preferred way to commute, by age group (% of respondents)

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 22% of respondents aged 18 to 34 preferred cycling, compared with only 5% of respondents aged 55 and older.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 61% of respondents aged 55 and older preferred driving.

choices.label: C
choices.text: among respondents aged 18 to 34, 22% preferred cycling, while 38% preferred driving.

choices.label: D
choices.text: public transit was preferred by similar shares of the two age groups, 27% and 24%.

content.explanation: The blank follows Petrovic's caution that cycling is not the younger group's top choice, so the data must show another option that more younger respondents preferred. Among those aged 18 to 34, 38% preferred driving and only 22% preferred cycling, as choice C says.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it supports Petrovic's first point (cycling is more popular with younger people), not her caution that it isn't their top choice.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it is about the older group, while the caution is about the younger group.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it doesn't compare cycling with any other option for the younger group.

passages.text: Musicologist Imani Brooks analyzed a sample of popular songs from four decades, measuring each song's tempo (in beats per minute) and length. Brooks argues that, across the decades in her sample, the length of popular songs changed far more than their tempo did.

table.title: Average tempo and length of popular songs in a sample

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Brooks's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The average song length was greatest in the 1980s, at 4.3 minutes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The average tempo stayed between 117 and 121 beats per minute in every decade, while the average length ranged from 2.8 to 4.3 minutes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The average tempo was slightly higher in the 2010s (120 beats per minute) than in the 2000s (117 beats per minute).

choices.label: D
choices.text: Songs from the 2010s were shorter on average than songs from the 2000s, at 3.5 minutes compared with 4.1 minutes.

content.explanation: Brooks compares how much two things changed: length and tempo. Choice B gives both ranges. Tempo varied by only 4 beats per minute (about 3%), while length varied from 2.8 to 4.3 minutes (a spread of 1.5 minutes, more than 50% of the shortest average). That shows length changed far more than tempo.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it describes only length and doesn't compare it with tempo.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it describes only tempo, in two decades, and doesn't compare it with length.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it describes only length, in two decades, and doesn't compare it with tempo.

passages.text: A student measured the vitamin C content of four fruits she bought at a local market. Oranges are often thought of as the best fruit source of vitamin C, so she was surprised to find that, among the fruits she tested, oranges were not the richest source: ______

choices.text: her strawberry samples contained 47 milligrams of vitamin C per 100 grams.

choices.label: B
choices.text: her apple samples contained the least vitamin C of the four fruits, 5 milligrams per 100 grams.

choices.label: C
choices.text: her orange samples contained 53 milligrams of vitamin C per 100 grams, far more than her apple samples did.

choices.label: D
choices.text: her kiwi samples contained 93 milligrams of vitamin C per 100 grams, compared with 53 milligrams in her orange samples.

distractorRationales.label: C

passages.text: Engineer Yusuf Demir tested four insulation panels by measuring how much heat passed through each one under identical conditions; less heat lost means better insulation. Demir claims that the choice of material can matter more than thickness, since a thin layer of a good insulating material can outperform a much thicker layer of a poorer one.

table.title: Heat lost through four insulation panels

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Demir's claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Panel 1, with 10 centimeters of fiberglass, lost about half as much heat as panel 2, with 5 centimeters of fiberglass.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Panel 4, with 5 centimeters of foam, lost less heat than panel 2, with 5 centimeters of fiberglass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Panel 3 lost less heat than any of the other panels.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Panel 3, with only 2 centimeters of aerogel, lost less heat than panel 1, with 10 centimeters of fiberglass.

content.explanation: Demir's claim is that a thin layer of a good material can beat a much thicker layer of a poorer one. Panel 3 (2 cm of aerogel) lost 16 watts, while panel 1 (10 cm of fiberglass, five times as thick) lost 18 watts. The thinner panel insulated better, which is exactly what choice D says.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true (18 watts vs. 34 watts), but it shows that thickness matters for the same material, which doesn't support the claim that material can matter more than thickness.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true and shows that material matters when thickness is equal, but it doesn't show a thin panel beating a much thicker one.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it doesn't mention thickness, so it doesn't show that panel 3 beat a thicker panel.

passages.text: A library that serves a large population can record many loans even if each resident borrows relatively little. Librarian Rosa Quint therefore argues that ranking libraries by their total number of loans can be misleading, and she points to four libraries in her region, where the library with the most loans is not the one whose residents borrow the most per person.

table.title: Population served and annual loans at four libraries

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Quint's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Northgate recorded 240,000 loans, more than any of the other three libraries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Westfield and Cedar Hill together served more people than Northgate did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elm Park, which serves 20,000 people, recorded 110,000 loans, while Northgate, which serves four times as many people, recorded only about twice as many loans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cedar Hill recorded 70,000 loans, the fewest of the four libraries, and served 35,000 people.

content.explanation: Quint's point is that the library with the most loans is not the one whose residents borrow the most per person. Northgate serves 4 times as many people as Elm Park (80,000 vs. 20,000) but records only about 2.2 times as many loans (240,000 vs. 110,000). So Elm Park residents borrow far more per person (5.5 loans each vs. 3 at Northgate), even though Northgate has the highest total. Choice C presents this comparison.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true and shows Northgate has the highest total, but it says nothing about population, so it can't show that the total is misleading.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true (85,000 vs. 80,000 people), but it compares populations only and says nothing about loans.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but Cedar Hill has both the fewest loans and the fewest loans per person (2 each), so its total is not misleading.

table.title: Shorebird nesting on four beaches

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: at Gannet Cove and Marram Beach, which ban dogs, an average of 1.8 and 1.5 chicks per nest survived to fly, compared with 0.6 and 0.9 at the two beaches that allow dogs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shoal Bay, which allows dogs, had 22 nests, the most of any beach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gannet Cove had fewer nests than Marram Beach did.

choices.label: D
choices.text: at Pell Point, which bans dogs, only 0.6 chicks per nest survived to fly.

The table shows the two beaches that ban dogs, Gannet Cove and Marram Beach, averaged 1.8 and 1.5 chicks fledged per nest. The two beaches that allow dogs, Pell Point and Shoal Bay, averaged only 0.6 and 0.9. Both dog-free beaches beat both dog-allowed beaches, so choice A completes the statement.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but the number of nests does not show how successful the nests were.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it compares two dog-free beaches with each other and gives no information about nest success.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The table shows that Pell Point allows dogs, so this misreads the table.

passages.text: Agronomist Rafael Ibáñez tested a new drip-irrigation schedule on three crops. He reports that the schedule reduced water use for every crop he tested, but he warns that it is not suitable for all crops, since for one crop the greatest water savings came at a real cost: ______

table.title: Results of a new irrigation schedule

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: corn used 520 liters of water per square meter under the old schedule but only 410 under the new one.

choices.label: B
choices.text: tomatoes, which had the largest drop in water use, from 600 to 450 liters per square meter, also had their yield fall by 12 percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: wheat's yield did not change even though its water use fell from 380 to 290 liters per square meter.

choices.label: D
choices.text: corn's yield rose by 2 percent, the largest gain of any crop.

content.explanation: The statement needs a crop whose water savings were the largest and also came with a cost. Find each crop's savings by subtracting. Corn: $520 - 410 = 110$ liters per square meter. Wheat: $380 - 290 = 90$. Tomatoes: $600 - 450 = 150$. So tomatoes saved the most water, and the table shows their yield changed by $-12\%$, a 12 percent drop. That drop is the cost, so choice B completes the statement.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but corn's yield rose, so its water savings came at no cost. Corn also did not have the largest savings.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it shows a crop that saved water with no loss in yield, the opposite of what the statement needs.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but a gain in yield is a benefit, not a cost, so it doesn't support Ibáñez's warning.

passages.text: For a health class project, a student surveyed her school about how many hours students sleep. She found that in every grade, students slept more on weekend nights than on school nights. For example, ______

table.title: Average hours of sleep per night, by grade

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ninth graders slept an average of 7.4 hours on school nights, the most of any grade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: twelfth graders slept less on school nights than tenth graders did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: tenth graders slept an average of 8.8 hours on school nights and 7.1 hours on weekend nights.

choices.label: D
choices.text: eleventh graders slept an average of 8.9 hours on weekend nights but only 6.8 hours on school nights.

content.explanation: The statement needs an example of one grade sleeping more on weekend nights than on school nights. The table shows eleventh graders averaged $8.9$ hours on weekend nights and $6.8$ hours on school nights, so they slept more on weekends. Choice D gives that example.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it compares school-night sleep across grades instead of comparing school nights with weekend nights.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it compares two grades on school nights only and says nothing about weekends.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This swaps the columns. Tenth graders slept 7.1 hours on school nights and 8.8 hours on weekend nights.

passages.text: Historian Wen Liang studied how grain reached the river city of Harwick in the nineteenth century. Liang argues that railroads replaced canals as the main route for grain shipments into the city during the 1860s: ______

table.title: Grain shipped into Harwick (thousands of tons)

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: canal shipments fell in every decade shown, from 410 thousand tons in 1850 to 160 thousand tons in 1880.

choices.label: B
choices.text: in 1860 canals carried 380 thousand tons of grain into the city and railroads only 150 thousand, but by 1870 railroads carried 310 thousand tons and canals 290 thousand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: rail shipments grew from 35 thousand tons in 1850 to 520 thousand tons in 1880.

choices.label: D
choices.text: by 1860 railroads were already carrying more grain into the city than canals were.

content.explanation: To show that railroads replaced canals during the 1860s, the data must show canals ahead at the start of the decade and railroads ahead at the end. In 1860, canals carried $380$ thousand tons and railroads $150$ thousand, so canals led. In 1870, railroads carried $310$ thousand tons and canals $290$ thousand, so railroads led. The switch happened between 1860 and 1870, so choice B completes the statement.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but a steady decline in canal shipments doesn't show when railroads overtook canals.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it doesn't compare railroads with canals or show that the change happened in the 1860s.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: In 1860 canals carried 380 thousand tons and railroads only 150 thousand, so this misreads the table.

passages.text: Education researcher Hollis Grant evaluated an after-school math tutoring program. He compared students in the program with similar students who were not, grouping both by their starting test scores and recording each group's average gain in points over the year. Grant concludes that the program's benefit was concentrated among students who began with the lowest scores.

table.title: Average gain in math test score over one year (points)

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Grant's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Students in the lowest third gained 14 points in the program versus 3 points without it, a difference of 11 points, while the differences for the middle and highest thirds were only 2 points and 1 point.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students in the program gained points in every starting-score group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students in the highest third who were in the program gained only 3 points, the smallest gain of any program group.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students in the middle third who were not in the program gained 4 points, more than students not in the program in either of the other groups.

content.explanation: The program's benefit for a group is the program gain minus the gain for similar students without the program. Lowest third: $14 - 3 = 11$ points. Middle third: $6 - 4 = 2$ points. Highest third: $3 - 2 = 1$ point. The benefit was $11$ points for the lowest group but only $2$ and $1$ for the others, so it was concentrated among the lowest scorers. Choice A uses exactly these comparisons.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but students without the program also gained points in every group, so gains alone don't show how much the program helped or where its benefit was concentrated.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it ignores the comparison group. To measure the program's benefit, each program gain must be compared with the gain of similar students outside the program.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it describes only students not in the program, so it says nothing about the program's benefit.

passages.text: A consumer magazine measured the power use and brightness of four household light bulbs. Its writers report that an LED bulb can match the brightness of a traditional incandescent bulb while using only a small fraction of the power: ______

table.title: Power use and brightness of four light bulbs

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the halogen bulb produced 750 lumens, the least light of any bulb tested.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the CFL bulb used 14 watts, more than the 9 watts used by the LED bulb.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the incandescent bulb used 60 watts to produce 800 lumens, more light than any other bulb produced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the LED bulb produced 800 lumens using 9 watts, while the incandescent bulb needed 60 watts to produce the same 800 lumens.

content.explanation: The statement compares the LED bulb with the incandescent bulb: same brightness, much less power. The table shows both produced $800$ lumens, but the LED used $9$ watts and the incandescent used $60$ watts. Since $\frac{9}{60} = 0.15$, the LED used only $15\%$ of the power. Choice D gives this comparison.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it is about the halogen bulb, not the LED or incandescent bulb.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it compares the LED with the CFL bulb, not with the incandescent bulb.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The incandescent, CFL and LED bulbs all produced 800 lumens, so the incandescent bulb did not produce more light than every other bulb. This misreads the table.

passages.text: The manager of Lindell Park tracked rainfall and the number of park visitors on four weekend days in June. She noticed that attendance dropped sharply on rainy days. For example, ______

table.title: Rainfall and visitors at Lindell Park

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the park had 1,100 visitors on June 10.

choices.label: B
choices.text: more rain fell on June 11 than on June 4.

choices.label: C
choices.text: on June 4, when 18 millimeters of rain fell, the park had 310 visitors, compared with 1,240 visitors on the dry day of June 3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: on June 11, when 25 millimeters of rain fell, the park had 1,240 visitors.

content.explanation: The statement needs an example comparing attendance on a rainy day with attendance on a dry day. On June 4, $18$ millimeters of rain fell and $310$ people visited. On June 3, no rain fell and $1{,}240$ people visited. Attendance was far lower on the rainy day, so choice C is the example.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it gives one day's attendance without any comparison to show that rain lowered it.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it compares rainfall only and says nothing about attendance.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The table shows the park had 270 visitors on June 11. The 1,240 visitors came on June 3, so this misreads the table.

passages.text: Book industry analyst Marguerite Oyelaran studied how readers in one country buy books in four genres. She found that the format readers prefer varies sharply by genre, and that romance stands apart from the others: ______

table.title: Share of sales by format and genre (%)

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: romance is the only genre in the table for which ebooks made up the majority of sales, at 62 percent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: children's books had the highest share of print sales, at 88 percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: mystery's ebook share of 45 percent was higher than biography's ebook share of 29 percent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: romance had the lowest ebook share of any genre, at 38 percent.

content.explanation: The statement needs data showing how romance differs from the other genres. Romance's ebook share is $62\%$, which is more than half of its sales. Every other genre has an ebook share below $50\%$ ($45\%$, $29\%$ and $12\%$). So romance is the only genre where ebooks outsell print, and choice A completes the statement.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it is about children's books, not about how romance stands apart.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it compares mystery with biography and says nothing about romance.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: The table shows romance's print share is 38 percent and its ebook share is 62 percent, the highest of any genre. This misreads the table.

passages.text: A city's express bus route skips many of the stops made by the local route along the same street. Transit planner Odile Marchetti argues that the express route's time advantage is real only outside rush hour; during the morning and evening rush, she says, traffic erases nearly all of it.

table.title: Average trip time from end to end (minutes)

content.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Marchetti's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The express trip was shorter than the local trip at every one of the four times measured.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The local trip took longest at 5:00 p.m., when it lasted 58 minutes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At 8:00 a.m., the express trip took 54 minutes, 26 minutes longer than it took at 6:00 a.m.

choices.label: D
choices.text: At 6:00 a.m. and 12:00 p.m., the express trip was 14 and 15 minutes shorter than the local trip, but at 8:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. it was only 1 minute shorter.

content.explanation: Marchetti's argument is about the express route's advantage, which is the local trip time minus the express trip time. At 6:00 a.m.: $42 - 28 = 14$ minutes. At 12:00 p.m.: $45 - 30 = 15$ minutes. At 8:00 a.m. (rush hour): $55 - 54 = 1$ minute. At 5:00 p.m. (rush hour): $58 - 57 = 1$ minute. The advantage is large outside rush hour and nearly gone during it, so choice D supports her argument.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it suggests the express route always has an advantage. It doesn't show that the advantage nearly disappears at rush hour.

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: This is true, but it describes only the local route, so it says nothing about the express route's advantage.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: This is true ($54 - 28 = 26$), but it shows only that the express bus slows down at rush hour. The local bus slows down too, so this alone doesn't show that the express route's advantage over the local route disappears.
